title: Multi-GPU Interconnect Study — NCCL Topology & Hybrid TP/Pipeline Observations
content:
Purpose:
This is a working-level log of experiments and profiling we ran to understand multi-GPU scaling limits in our serving runtime. Focus: how NCCL topology, interconnect (NVLink / PCIe / RoCE), and hybrid parallelism (tensor parallel + pipeline parallel within a single model forward) affect tail latency and throughput for short-to-medium sequence workloads (seq len 64-512).

Background / motivation:
- Customers expect predictable per-request latency at low batch sizes (1-8) but we also need to saturate hardware for peak throughput.
- Our runtime supports dynamic sharding (tensor parallelism via XLA-like sharding and pipeline stages), but we've seen non-linear slowdowns when moving from 4->8 GPUs in some racks.
- Hypothesis: suboptimal NCCL topology selection + inter-node link saturation + host-side thread scheduling are primary contributors.

Testbed summary (hardware/software):
- Nodes: 2x DGX-ish nodes (8x A100 GPUs each) connected by Mellanox Spectrum-based 100Gb/s RoCE (RDMA) and NVLink within-node.
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04, NVIDIA driver 535.x, CUDA 12.x, NCCL 2.18.
- Runtime build: redwood-runtime rev 7b12c (branch: perf/multi-gpu), built with CUDA-aware NCCL and GDR support enabled.
- Tools used: nsys (Nsight Systems) for timeline traces, nv-nsight-cu (ncu) for kernel-level hotspots, perf for CPU sampling, ibv_devinfo and mlnx_tune for NIC diagnostics, nccl-tests (all_reduce_perf) for microbenchmarks.

Experiment matrix (high-level):
- Scope: single-node 4 vs 8 GPUs, and two-node 8+8 GPUs.
- Variables: NCCL SOCKETS vs RING topologies, NCCL_ALGO (TREE vs RING), CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES ordering, CPU affinity (numactl pinning), GDR_COPY=1/0, XLA-like tensor partitioning degree, pipeline stage counts.
- Metrics: p50/p90/p99 latency for single-request generation of 128 tokens (batch=1, prompt=32), tokens/sec aggregated, NCCL bandwidth/utilization, CPU sys/us times, PCIe link utilization.

Representative commands: (run with RDW env wrappers in perf lab)
- microbandwidth: LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/libnccl.so NCCL_DEBUG=INFO ./all_reduce_perf -b 8 -e 4G -f 2 -g 8
- distributed run: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0 python -m torch.distributed.run --nproc_per_node=8 --nnodes=2 --node_rank=0 serve_perf.py --seq_len 128 --batch 1 --tp 2 --pp 2
- trace capture: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt -o trace-8gpu ./serve_perf_runner.sh

Key observations (short bullets):
1) Single-node (NVLink within) scaling 2x->4x is near-linear for our tensor-parallel sharding. Going 4->8 on the same node shows ~1.6x improvement, not 2x. NCCL shows micro-pauses around collective sync points.
2) Multi-node (8+8 via RoCE) scaling is much worse for small batches: p99 latency increases by ~2.5x vs single-node 8-gpu baseline. Bandwidth per GPU drops ~60% compared to within-node NVLink.
3) NCCL topology choice matters: default topology for our card/driver sometimes selects cross-host rings that force data on the slow RoCE links even when host-local NVLink paths exist. Forcing local-first topologies improves p99 by ~18% for mixed-node runs.
4) Small message inefficiencies: for per-token KV cache exchanges (many small allgather/allreduce) NCCL tree algorithms outperform ring for p99, but ring gives better aggregate bandwidth for large tensors.
5) CPU scheduling: observed frequent context switches in the Python worker process on multi-node runs; pinning critical threads (nccl threads + python worker) to isolated cores reduced jitter.

Representative measured numbers (from runs on 2024-11-10):
- all_reduce_perf (8 GPUs single-node, large msg 256MB per GPU): 140 GB/s aggregate
- all_reduce_perf (8 GPUs across 2 nodes): 38 GB/s aggregate (100GbE/RoCE overhead + NIC buffering)
- Model workload (batch=1, seq=128): tokens/sec: single-node-8: 4200 t/s; two-node-16: 5400 t/s (inefficient scaling), p99 latency single-node-8: 220 ms, two-node-16: 560 ms.
(These numbers are specific to our test model and the roofline for our infra; absolute numbers are for diagnosis not shipping claims.)

Deep-dive profiling snippets and interpretation:
- nsys timeline: spikes align with NCCL allreduce windows and with CPU-side GIL release/rehold points. We saw ~40-80ms periods where GPUs are idle waiting on host-driven collectives.
- ncu results: top kernels are fused-attn forward/backward and a custom KV-copy kernel. Kernel occupancy is good, but memcpy/host->device small copies dominate when using pipeline stages that frequently exchange small KV chunks.
- NCCL debug logs: messages indicating fallback to P2P on certain links and repeated retries on error counters when NIC driver offloads were saturated (see RDW-1342).

Hypotheses validated / rejected:
- H1: Topology selection causes cross-host traffic even for local reductions. VALID. Forcing NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME and setting NCCL_TOPO_DUMP helped diagnose; explicit NCCL_TOPO_COLL tree config improved locality.
- H2: NIC saturation is primary limiter for two-node runs. PARTIALLY VALID. NIC bandwidth is a limiter, but inefficiencies in message aggregation (many small messages) amplify effect. Aggregating messages reduced p99 much more than raw NIC tuning.
- H3: GDR and CUDA IPC cause stalls. MIXED. GDR reduces copy overhead for large tensors but for many small buffers GDR overheads plus driver work creates overhead; batching of all small KV exchanges into fewer larger messages helps more than toggling GDR alone.

Changes tried and impact summary (most impactful first):
- Message aggregation (coalesce small KV updates into 4–8MB chunks): p99 down ~30-45% for two-node runs.
- Force local NCCL hierarchy via NCCL_TOPO: p99 down ~18% for mixed racks; tokens/sec up ~12%.
- CPU pinning (numactl --physcpubind): p99 jitter reduced by ~10–20ms; system CPU contention improved.
- Turning off GDR_COPY for our workload: small improvement in tail for small-message heavy runs; degraded large-batch throughput slightly.

Open questions / TODOs (actionable):
- Q1: Can we change runtime scheduling to coalesce KV exchanges automatically per-request without user changes? (Spike: add a coalescer layer at the RPC boundary.)
- Q2: Should we detect topology at startup and set NCCL_TOPO envs automatically for Dedicated clusters? (Tied to RDW-OPS & provisioning)
- Q3: For multi-node routes, evaluate using 200GbE or HDR InfiniBand — how much would that reduce p99? Need one-shot test on perf lab with 200G NICs.
- Q4: Investigate enabling IPC + CUDA Multi-Process Service (MPS) under certain configurations to reduce host CPU overhead.

Immediate next steps assigned:
- Marcus: automate NCCL topology dump and a quick-check script that fails fast if topology would route locally-avoidable traffic across NICs (RDW-1342 follow-up). Due: 2024-11-22.
- Sofia: implement a prototype message coalescer in the runtime (coalesce KV exchanges per request up to 8MB). Validate on single-node and two-node tests. Due: 2024-11-29.
- Aisha (me): add perf lab ticket to request 200GbE NICs for one-day benchmarking window and run the same experiment matrix; log results to RDW-OPS. Due: 2024-12-06.

Notes / miscellany (scratch):
- Found weird NCCL debug lines: "NCCL WARN P2P fallback (cudaErrorIllegalAddress)" on one run — likely driver bug or run-to-run memory corruption; re-ran with a clean reboot, didn't reappear. Keep an eye.
- Found that disabling hyperthreading on hosts reduced CPU scheduling jitter in these experiments.
- Linked PR: runtime change that adds an env var REDWOOD_COALESCE_KV (experimental) is at https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/481 — review TODO.

Raw attachments (traces saved in perf-lab):
- /perf-lab/traces/multi-node/trace-20241110-8gpu.nsys
- /perf-lab/ncu/results/ncu-run-20241110.txt

Conclusion (working):
- Primary levers to improve tail and scaling for mixed NVLink+RoCE clusters: ensure NCCL picks local-first topologies, coalesce small inter-GPU messages on the runtime side, and apply CPU thread isolation. Longer-term: upgrade interconnects for two-node heavy workloads or provide an explicit "single-node-optimized" placement constraint for customer workloads that need tight latency SLOs.

If you want raw logs/NSYS captures, ping me or look at the perf-lab bucket. This doc will be turned into a formal postmortem / runbook if the coalescer prototype shows promising results.

---
Notes to self: keep this doc informal; copy into a confluence page once we have final numbers and recommended runtime knobs to expose to customers (e.g., REDWOOD_COALESCE_KV, REDWOOD_NCCL_LOCALFIRST).
